summary.headline: A good glove maker with a better 2026, but at Rs 59.70 the price is about 50% above our fair value of Rs 39.40
summary.text:
Dipped Products PLC (DIPD.N0000), 42% owned by Hayleys (49% with Haycarb), is one of the world's big makers of rubber gloves for households, industry and medical use, with factories in Sri Lanka and Thailand. It also owns controlling stakes in three tea and rubber plantation companies (Kelani Valley, Talawakelle and Horana), which bring in 38% of revenue. Profit to shareholders rose 53% to Rs 2.75bn in April–September 2026, with glove profit up 44% on new capacity, while plantations earned 17% less.

Fair value is about **Rs 39.40** (buy below **Rs 33.49**, strong buy below **Rs 29.55**). The gap comes from returns: shareholders should demand about 17.3% a year (beta 0.88), and the company has earned 10–15% on equity for three years. At an ROE of 14% the shares are worth about 0.73× book, against 0.97× today.

3 of the 4 business tests pass (debt, steady profit, cash); returns fail. Category 2: watch list. Debt has risen to fund a big capex programme (Rs 7.8bn in 2025/26, Rs 4.2bn more in the half), and dividends were not covered by cash after capex last year.

valuation.note: Fair value weights the bear/base/bull values of five methods 30/50/20 and averages them: whole-company DCF less minorities plus investments (Rs 31.04), P/E (45.61), justified P/B (45.19), residual income (38.74) and dividends (36.44). NAV (Rs 61.72) is a reading only.

models.comment: Whole-company DCF at WACC 14.3% / 13.3% / 12.2%: after-tax operating profit Rs 5.17bn (twelve-month segment operating profit to Sep 2026, Rs 7.64bn, at the 2025/26 tax rate of 32.4%), start cash after maintenance capex Rs 3.95 / 5.45 / 5.45bn (plus depreciation and amortisation Rs 3.37bn, less maintenance Rs 4.59 / 3.09 / 3.09bn), growth 3% / 6% / 8% for five years then 4% / 5% / 6%, return on new capital 11% / 13% / 15%; less net debt Rs 16.24bn; then less the minorities' book value (Rs 9.01bn) plus other financial assets (Rs 3.35bn), −Rs 9.46 a share. In the bear case the return on new capital is below WACC, so growth destroys value and the equity is worth about nothing; 71% of the base value and 80% of the bull value come after year 5.

Today's 8.0× trailing P/E is above the bull case.

models.name: Justified price to book
models.comment: NAV Rs 61.72 (30 Sep 2026) × (long-run ROE − growth) ÷ (cost of equity − growth): ROE 11% / 14% / 17%, growth 4% / 5% / 6%. Justified P/B 0.47 / 0.73 / 1.12 against 0.97 today.

models.name: Residual income
models.comment: Book Rs 61.72; ROE moving from 12.6% (twelve months to Sep 2026) to 11% / 14% / 17% over ten years; 30% payout; then excess returns grow at 4% / 5% / 6%. At the base 17.3% cost of equity, every ROE case below 17% is worth less than book.

models.name: Dividend model
models.comment: Dividend to March 2027 Rs 2.3 / 2.6 / 2.9 (Rs 1.33 already paid), growing 3% / 6% / 8% for five years, then the stable payout 1 − growth ÷ ROE (64% in the base case) on EPS Rs 7.5 / 8.9 / 9.6 grown at the same rates, long-run growth 4% / 5% / 6%. Growth is within the 6.4% supported by profit kept × ROE.

modelsNote: Five methods are averaged in each scenario: whole-company DCF less minorities plus investments, P/E, justified price to book, residual income and the dividend model. Growth check: the calculator's supported growth (27.9%, from a 2025/26 reinvestment of 210% of after-tax operating profit) isn't a steady figure, so profit kept × ROE (63.8% × 10.1% = 6.4%) is the check; base 6% and bull 8% are within 2 points, bull backed by the Katunayake plant under construction. Maintenance capex: no company split; 2025/26 capex (Rs 7.78bn) was mostly growth, so base and bull use depreciation (Rs 3.09bn) and bear the calculator's middle (Rs 4.59bn). Ratio notes: the 6.6% cost of debt is below the usual range because much of the debt is in dollars, baht and euros (the report's capitalisation rate is 7.7%); the 32.4% tax rate of 2025/26 is above the 30% standard rate because of plantation losses and disallowed costs, and the April–September 2026 rate (21.8%) was lower. Base EPS (Rs 8.9) is 12% below the September quarter × 4 because that quarter's tax was only 18%. Dividends were more than cash after maintenance capex in 2025/26: flagged as at risk.

scenarios.common: Required return from CAPM with a country premium: risk-free 8.24% (12.24% bond less 4.0% default spread), mature premium 4.2% plus country premium 6.08%, beta 0.88. Weights bear 30 / base 50 / bull 20. Net debt Rs 16.24bn, NAV Rs 61.72, minorities Rs 9.01bn and other financial assets Rs 3.35bn at 30 Sep 2026; 598.6mn shares.

sensitivity.title: Residual income, Rs per share
sensitivity.note: Starting ROE 12.6%, growth 5%, payout 30%. Rs 59.70 needs a long-run ROE of about 19% at the base cost of equity, or about 16–17% at 15.8%.

buyPlan.note: About Rs 17,336 in total, against Rs 29,850 at Rs 59.70. The business is good enough to own (category 2), but not at today's price.
buyPlan.realism: The buy price Rs 33.49 is 44% below Rs 59.70. The share hasn't traded that low since early 2024 (Rs 30.40 at March 2024); its lows were Rs 45.90 in April–June 2025, Rs 46.70 in 2025/26 and Rs 49.30 in April–September 2026. Reaching it would take a market fall or a glove downturn, so it is unlikely in the next year; the first tier (Rs 39.40) is also below anything seen since 2024.

higher: Glove profit keeping its 40%+ growth into 2027 as the Katunayake plant starts, lifting ROE back above 15%.
Plantations recovering with better weather and tea and rubber prices.
Receivables and short-term loans coming back down, so cash after capex covers dividends again.
A lower cost of equity (a lower bond yield or country premium).
lower: Debt rising further to fund Katunayake and working capital (net debt already up Rs 4.6bn in six months).
Glove price competition from Malaysian, Thai and Chinese makers, or US tariffs on Sri Lankan and Thai goods.
Plantation wage increases without matching tea and rubber prices.
The low September-quarter tax rate not repeating.

notes.disclaimer: These are estimates from the annual report to March 2026 and the interim reports to June and September 2026. This is analysis, not personal financial advice.

fullText:
**Dipped Products PLC (DIPD.N0000): first analysis, 25 November 2026**

**Summary.** A good glove maker, but the price is well above what it earns on its capital. Fair value is about **Rs 39.40**. The buy price is **Rs 33.49** and the strong buy **Rs 29.55**, against Rs 59.70 (last trade, 30 September 2026). 3 of the 4 business tests pass, so the category is **2: watch list**. The case for the share is that the glove business is growing fast again and new capacity is coming. The case against is that return on equity has been 10–15% for three years, below the 17.3% a shareholder should demand. Debt is also rising to pay for the expansion.

**The business.** Hayleys PLC owns 42.12% and its subsidiary Haycarb another 6.80%. The group has two parts:
- **Hand protection** (62% of 2025/26 revenue, 63% of segment profit). Household, industrial, medical, sports and disposable gloves from five plants in Sri Lanka and two in Thailand. About 99% is exported, with 56% of glove sales going to Europe and 16% to North America. Italian, French and Polish sales arms (ICOGUANTI, DPL France, Rozenbal) sell under the group's own brands.
- **Plantations** (38% of revenue). Controlling stakes in Kelani Valley, Talawakelle and Horana Plantations: tea and rubber on about 65,000 acres. They also supply some of the latex the gloves need.

Minorities own Rs 9.0bn of the group's Rs 46.0bn equity, mostly in the plantation companies, and took 24% of 2025/26 profit.

**Results.**

| | 2021/22 | 2022/23 | 2023/24 | 2024/25 | 2025/26 | Apr–Sep 2025 | Apr–Sep 2026 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue, Rs bn | 55.3 | 80.1 | 73.9 | 79.3 | 82.0 | 43.5 | 50.4 |
| Profit before tax, Rs bn | 7.60 | 11.22 | 7.57 | 6.84 | 6.83 | 3.25 | 3.99 |
| Profit to shareholders, Rs bn | 5.38 | 6.51 | 4.47 | 3.88 | 3.52 | 1.80 | 2.75 |
| EPS, Rs | 8.99 | 10.87 | 7.47 | 6.47 | 5.88 | 3.01 | 4.59 |
| ROE (company) | 24.6% | 24.1% | 15.5% | 12.2% | 10.1% | | 12.6% (12 months) |
| Dividend, Rs | 2.50 | 3.00 | 2.25 | 1.90 | 2.13 | 0.86 | 1.33 |

Profit fell for three years after the pandemic glove boom, then turned up in 2026/27. In April–September 2026:
- Glove revenue rose 22% to Rs 34.1bn and glove segment profit 44% to Rs 3.27bn. The new W3 plant at Hanwella (opened April 2025) and Hi-Care Thai Gloves (bought December 2024) added capacity.
- Plantation revenue rose 4%, but segment profit fell 17% to Rs 0.89bn, on wages and weather.
- Tax was only 21.8% of profit before tax (32.8% a year earlier), and only 18% in the September quarter. That flatters the half's 53% rise in profit to shareholders.

**Balance sheet and cash.** Net debt was Rs 2.9bn in March 2025, Rs 11.6bn in March 2026 and **Rs 16.2bn** at 30 September 2026. That is 0.44× owners' equity and 1.5× twelve-month EBITDA. Three things drove it:
- Capex: Rs 7.8bn in 2025/26 (gloves Rs 5.8bn, plantations Rs 2.0bn) and Rs 4.4bn in the half, against depreciation of about Rs 3.1bn a year. Another Rs 3.4bn is contracted and Rs 2.1bn approved.
- Working capital: Rs 5.0bn in 2025/26 and Rs 3.4bn in the half, mostly customers paying later. Receivables reached Rs 22.6bn.
- Dividends: Rs 1.68bn in 2025/26 including minorities, more than operating cash after depreciation-level upkeep (Rs 0.73bn). So the dividend was in effect borrowed. It is flagged as at risk until working capital stops growing.

Short-term loans and overdrafts are Rs 12.65bn of the Rs 19.8bn borrowed. Interest costs rose 56% in the half to Rs 0.94bn. The group also holds Rs 3.35bn of other financial assets (fixed deposits, a Singer Finance subordinated trust and Martin Bauer Hayleys shares).

**Required return.** The beta is 0.88. Damodaran's global unlevered betas for rubber products (0.78) and farming (0.49) are weighted 63/37 by segment profit, then relevered for DPL's debt. The figure is provisional, because his emerging-markets file couldn't be opened and no local 5-year beta was found. Cost of equity is 8.24% + 0.88 × (4.2% + 6.08%) = **17.3%** (bear 18.8%, bull 15.8%). Debt costs only 6.6% before tax, because much of it is in dollars, baht and euros. Debt is 31% of the company's value, so WACC is 13.3% (14.3% / 12.2%).

**Methods (Rs a share).**

| Method | Bear | Base | Bull | Weighted |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DCF less minorities plus investments | −0.19 | 36.88 | 63.30 | 31.04 |
| P/E | 32.25 | 46.52 | 63.39 | 45.61 |
| Justified P/B | 29.19 | 45.16 | 69.28 | 45.19 |
| Residual income | 24.18 | 37.98 | 62.49 | 38.74 |
| Dividend model | 23.38 | 36.91 | 54.84 | 36.44 |
| Average | 21.76 | 40.69 | 62.66 | **39.40** |

- **DCF**: the whole group is valued, then net debt (Rs 16.24bn) and the minorities' book value (Rs 9.01bn) come off, and the other financial assets (Rs 3.35bn) are added.
  - Inputs: after-tax operating profit Rs 5.17bn (twelve-month segment profit Rs 7.64bn at 32.4% tax); growth 3% / 6% / 8% for five years, then 4% / 5% / 6%; return on new capital 11% / 13% / 15%.
  - In the bear case new capital earns less than WACC and upkeep is costlier, so the equity is worth about nothing.
  - 71% of the base value and 80% of the bull value come after year 5.
- **P/E**: EPS to March 2027 of Rs 7.5 / 8.9 / 9.6 (Rs 4.59 already earned), at justified P/Es of 4.3 / 5.2 / 6.6. The September quarter × 4 gives Rs 10.12. The base is 12% below that because the quarter's tax rate (18%) is unlikely to last: at 30% the quarter is about Rs 2.17, × 4 = Rs 8.7.
- **P/B and residual income**: book Rs 61.72, with ROE settling at 11% / 14% / 17% from today's 12.6%. The justified P/B is 0.47 / 0.73 / 1.12 against 0.97 today. Rs 59.70 needs a long-run ROE of about 19%.
- **Dividends**: Rs 2.3 / 2.6 / 2.9 for 2026/27 (Rs 1.33 already paid), then the stable payout.
- **Growth check**: profit kept × ROE (63.8% × 10.1%) supports 6.4% a year. Base (6%) and bull (8%) are within 2 points; the bull case is backed by the Katunayake plant under construction. The calculator's capex-based figure (27.9%) comes from one exceptional year of reinvestment (210% of after-tax operating profit) and isn't used.
- **Maintenance capex**: the company gives no split. 2025/26 capex (Rs 7.78bn) was 2.5× depreciation, and the report describes it as expansion: the Katunayake greenfield plant, W3 at Hanwella and capacity at Kottawa and Hanwella Rubber. So it is mostly growth, to be judged on its return. Base and bull use depreciation (Rs 3.09bn) as upkeep; the bear case uses Rs 4.59bn.
- **NAV** (Rs 61.72) is shown as a reading only. It includes plantation land and bearer plants, which earn little on their book value.

**Business tests (3 of 4).**
- Debt: pass (0.44×), but rising fast.
- Steady profit: pass. There was no loss in five years and no large one-offs, though profit fell three years running from the boom.
- Cash: pass. Operating cash matched profit 1.1× over 2024/25–2025/26, though it was weak in the latest half (Rs 0.93bn against Rs 3.12bn profit), and free cash after capex was negative.
- Returns: fail. ROE was 15.5%, 12.2% and 10.1% in the last three years and 12.6% over the latest twelve months.

**Buy plan (500 shares).** Buy 200 at up to Rs 39.40, 150 at up to Rs 33.49 and 150 at up to Rs 29.55: about Rs 17,336, an average of Rs 34.67. The share hasn't been below Rs 45 since early 2024 (Rs 30.40 at March 2024). Its 2026/27 range so far is Rs 49.30–62.40, so the buy price is unlikely to be reached without a market fall or a glove downturn.

**Management.** Management's message is growth in higher-value gloves: Katunayake, Thailand, automation and new products. The glove numbers so far back it up. What is less convincing is the funding. Debt to equity rose from 0.40 to about 0.49 in six months, and the report gives no cost or completion date for the Katunayake plant. Plantations remain the weak side.

**What would change the view.** Higher: glove profit growth continuing into 2027 so ROE gets back above 15%; plantations recovering; receivables and short-term debt coming down; a lower cost of equity. Lower: more debt; glove price competition or US tariffs; plantation wage rises; the low tax rate not lasting.

**Uncertain.**
- The price is the 30 September 2026 last trade, because the CSE site couldn't be reached from this run and the share isn't yet in the site's price file. The site's daily close will replace it.
- The beta is a global stand-in.
- The report names its growth projects but not their cost, so maintenance capex is a judgement.
- Depreciation here leaves out the moulds (formers), whose wear is already charged in operating profit.
